Life from age 4 to 16

I like practicing until a sequence makes sense with the rest of the team. I do not know how I would feel in a real emergency, and I want to understand the hours and responsibilities before I make a bigger decision.

  • family: Lives with parents and an older brother.
  • finances: Moderate income; practical training costs need comparison.
  • geography: San Angelo, Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: English; family takes part in local volunteer events.
  • school: Public high school with access to an introductory first-aid course.
  • accessOpportunities: Instructor-led scenarios only; no independent emergency care.
  • Age 4–5

    In 2014, Jordan liked relay games and inventing sequences everyone had to follow. She also drew colorful maps for imagined islands, usually leaving the destination undecided until the rest of the game was already underway.

  • Age 6–7

    At six, she began helping arrange supplies for community events. During 2017, she learned that being ready for a task could involve several unexciting checks, and that skipping one sometimes created extra work for another person.

  • Age 8–9

    In 2018, Jordan joined a recreation team and liked rehearsing coordinated moves. She was not always calm in ordinary disagreements, but found it easier to focus when the group shared a specific task and practiced it beforehand.

  • Age 10–11

    During 2020, she helped household members keep track of changing school routines. She liked clear instructions and practical assistance, while long online discussions with no next step often left her restless and unsure how to contribute.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve, Jordan became curious about first aid through a community demonstration. In 2023, she asked about the difference between introductory practice and the training required before someone could take responsibility for an actual emergency.

  • Age 14–15

    Across 2024 and 2025, she attended an introductory first-aid course and repeated scenarios with an instructor. Immediate trained care and team procedures appealed more than years of diagnostic follow-up, though she had never independently helped in an emergency.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen in 2026, Jordan is investigating Texas EMT courses and related training. She is willing to examine varied hours rather than assuming she will tolerate them, and values practical service more than expensive travel or an impressive-sounding role.

Life now

  • enjoys: First-aid practice · Repeated procedures · Coordinated team tasks
  • avoids: Long discussions without a next step · Assuming scenarios predict crisis performance
  • activities: Introductory first-aid course · Instructor-led scenarios
  • demonstratedSkills: Follows practiced sequences · Checks course supplies
  • unfamiliarActivities: Independent emergency care · Real crisis conditions · Shift-work routines
  • motivations: Practical service · Being prepared
  • ambitions: Investigate EMT and related introductory training · She imagines a dependable home life, useful work, and ordinary time with people she trusts.
  • struggles: Limited real-world exposure · Restlessness when tasks are unclear
  • supports: Parents · Course instructor · School adviser
  • practicalConstraints: Age and entry requirements need checking · Transport · Training fees

Still uncertain: How would real unpredictability affect her? · What work hours and training demands would fit her life?

Conditional plan preview

Conditional preview of the first displayed career, to test preparation and money. This is not a student choice or a correct-career answer key.

Career: Emergency Medical Technicians

Preparation: Texas DSHS EMT certification.

  • At least 18 with a high school diploma or GED.
  • Complete an approved EMT course and National Registry requirements.
  • Apply to DSHS and complete fingerprinting.

Training budget before aid: $13,221 · 0.3 study years in this reference

Still needs funding: $13,221 · loan payments $0/month · included in lifestyle: no

Annual pay before tax: $37,056 · TWC entry-wage proxy · entry

Chosen-life income range: $60,000–$75,000

Budget result: This pay does not cover your lifestyle. Your costs and savings are higher than your take-home pay.

Financial assumptions: Supported wishes: dependable home life, practical service and ordinary social time; expensive travel is not a priority. Used transport and every precise category level are modest single-adult references, not assumptions that a training path will fund them.
